title: Report: Honda to Offer Body-on-Frame Pickup in U.S. Thanks to Mitsubishi
summary: Body-on-frame pickups are such a big deal in the U.S. that everybody wants a share of the pie—even Honda, based on a recent report from Automotive News. body_markdown:
Body-on-frame pickups are such a big deal in the U.S. that everybody wants a share of the pie—even Honda, based on a recent ** report from *[Automotive News](https://www.autonews.com/honda/an-honda-sourcing-mitsubishi-triton-pickup-1009/)* . According to Japanese newspapers *Yomiuri* and *Nikkei* , the Japanese automaker synonymous with affordable sedans like the Civic and Accord will offer a ladder-frame, mid-size pickup in the U.S. market in 2028.


Two years is awfully short when it comes to car-development timelines. Therefore, Honda is expected to partner with Mitsubishi to bring to market a version of an existing model, the Triton pickup. That truck is sold around the world, including Southeast Asia and Australia, and is about the same size as Honda’s current midsizer, the unibody Ridgeline. (The Triton is about five inches narrower—that’s the biggest difference.) If Honda does bring a[badge-engineered](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/are-badge-engineered-cars-a-better-value/) version of the Triton to the U.S., it would compete against the Ford Ranger, the Chevrolet Colorado, and the Toyota Tacoma.


Toyota


Chevrolet


Ford


Mitsubishi


The most obvious way that the Triton could differentiate itself against these proven rivals is a diesel powertrain. After the Chevy Colorado dropped its diesel option[for the 2023 model year](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/all-new-2023-chevy-colorado-hones-off-road-image/) , compression-ignition disappeared from the mid-size truck segment in the U.S., and hasn’t returned. As of the 2023 update, the Triton is offered *only* with diesel power thanks to a 2.4-liter turbocharged inline-four available in three different tunes. Honda’s Ridgeline is powered by a 3.5-liter V-6 making 280 hp and 262 lb-ft of torque; it’s paired with a nine-speed automatic and capable of towing 5000 pounds.


Mitsubishi


In Australia, the Triton comes in 4×2 or 4×4 variants, with single-, club-, and double-cab setups. Suspension is double wishbones with coil springs and stabilizer bars up front and leaf springs out back. The bed size of the Triton Double Cab, the model we expect to see here, is 61.2 inches long by 60.8 inches wide, making it about 3 inches longer and one inch narrower than the bed of the Ridgeline.


Why would Honda want to expand its truck portfolio to include a body-on-frame model, when it has resisted doing so even when Nissan and Toyota got in the game decades ago? In short, it needs the money. This spring, Honda posted its first loss since it went public … in 1957. Not only did it post a $9B write-down earlier this year, due to restructuring its electric-vehicle business, but its sales in China are collapsing: “Honda’s local sales shrank to 645,000 vehicles in 2025 from a peak of 1.63 million in 2020, according to numbers from the Japanese carmaker’s China subsidiary Honda Motor Investment China,” says *Auto News* .


What would you like to see in a Mitsubishi-Triton-turned-Honda pickup? If Honda does indeed bring a Triton to our shores, we’re most curious about the powertrains and the packaging, especially because the Ridgeline is an excellent example of the latter. Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.
